audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet Jehoiakim vassalage, Babylonian regional attacks, Jehoiachin siege and deportation, temple plunder, skilled-worker exile, and Zedekiah installation narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for Babylonian vassalage and rebellion, raiding bands, theological attribution to Manasseh, innocent blood, imperial transfer from Egypt to Babylon, adolescent king and queen mother, siege and surrender, temple dismantling, elite and skilled-worker deportation, poorest residents left, forced renaming, puppet kingship, and renewed rebellion.

verses.restored: In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon went up, and Jehoiakim became his servant three years; then he turned and rebelled against him.

YHWH sent against him bands of Chaldeans, bands of Arameans, bands of Moab, and bands of children of Ammon; he sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to word of YHWH spoken through his servants the prophets.
Surely by mouth of YHWH this came upon Judah, to remove it from before his face, because of sins of Manasseh according to all he did,
and also innocent blood he shed, for he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and YHWH was unwilling to forgive.
Remaining acts of Jehoiakim and all he did, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Judah?
Jehoiakim lay with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son became king in his place.
King of Egypt did not again go out from his land, for king of Babylon had taken from wadi of Egypt to river Euphrates all that belonged to king of Egypt.
Eighteen years old was Jehoiachin when he became king, and three months he reigned in Jerusalem. Name of his mother was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan from Jerusalem.
He did evil in eyes of YHWH, according to all his father had done.
At that time servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon went up against Jerusalem, and city entered siege.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against city while his servants were besieging it.
Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to king of Babylon, he, his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officers. King of Babylon took him in eighth year of his reign.
He brought out from there all treasures of house of YHWH and treasures of king's house, and cut apart all vessels of gold Solomon king of Israel had made in temple of YHWH, as YHWH had spoken.
He exiled all Jerusalem, all commanders, and all mighty warriors—ten thousand exiles—and every craftworker and smith; none remained except poorest of people of land.
He exiled Jehoiachin to Babylon, and king's mother, king's wives, his officers, and mighty ones of land he led into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.
All men of might, seven thousand, and craftworkers and smiths, one thousand, all strong and trained for war—king of Babylon brought them into exile to Babylon.
King of Babylon made Mattaniah, his father's brother, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Twenty-one years old was Zedekiah when he became king, and eleven years he reigned in Jerusalem. Name of his mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did evil in eyes of YHWH, according to all Jehoiakim had done.
For through anger of YHWH this happened in Jerusalem and Judah until he cast them from before his face. Then Zedekiah rebelled against king of Babylon.

translation_notes: Babylonian vassalage, tribute, and rebellion are imperial politics. Jehoiakim's choices matter, but populations living beneath him bear raids, siege, taxation, and retaliation.
The raiding bands include Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites. These ancient labels may not become inherited guilt or hostility toward modern peoples.

The narrator attributes Judah's removal to Manasseh and innocent blood shed in an earlier reign. This collective and intergenerational punishment theology is morally dangerous and cannot justify harming descendants.
The refusal to 'forgive' innocent blood should center the murdered victims and institutional impunity, not make later civilians payment for crimes they did not commit.
Jehoiachin is eighteen and reigns three months. His mother Nehushta, wives, officers, and household surrender with him and are deported; they are people under coercion, not royal baggage.
Temple treasure and historic gold vessels are dismantled and removed. Imperial conquest includes cultural and religious extraction.

Ten thousand people are deported, with commanders, soldiers, craftworkers, and smiths specifically targeted. Skilled-worker removal weakens the occupied society while transferring knowledge to empire.
Those described as poorest remain in land. They are not disposable leftovers; they inherit devastated infrastructure, coerced agriculture, and political vulnerability.
Mattaniah is installed and renamed Zedekiah by Babylon. Forced renaming marks imperial control over identity and puppet sovereignty.
Numbers and chronology differ across Kings, Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Babylonian evidence and require source-witness audit.
safety_note: Do not blame later civilians for Manasseh, stigmatize ancient or modern ethnic groups, romanticize surrender or rebellion, treat deportees as elite abstractions, or dismiss those left behind as merely poor. Center innocent-blood accountability without collective punishment, the queen mother and families, cultural plunder, skilled-worker extraction, forced renaming, and empire's control over both exiles and survivors.
